To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

transplantation of neonatal rat pancreas under the kidney capsule in alloxan induced diabetic rats restores glucose tolerance to glucose ingestion and that the restoration is dependent on a load-dependent potentiation of glucose-stimulated insulin release and an anticipatory nervoulsy triggered insulin release.

In rats with alloxan induced pancreas destruction and regeneration of a small part of their original pancreatic mass, transplantation of neonatally derived pancreatic grafts under the kidney capsule restored the normal insulin response to ingestion of 750 mg glucose.

transplantation of neonatal rat pancreases under the renal capsule is a suitable experimental model for the study of the effects of pancreas transplantation upon the insulin responses to oral glucose ingestion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of the pancreas transplantation on the glucose induced insulin secretion.
the effect of pancreas transplantation upon the glucose induced insulin release and upon the insulin secretion in response to oral glucose ingestion in the rat.
the effects of transplantation of neonatal rat pancreases on the glucose tolerance curve to oral glucose ingestion in rats with alloxan induced insulinopenic diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transplantation of a neonatal pancreas under the kidney capsule in alloxan induced diabetic rats, leads to an improved glucose tolerance curve.
the insulin response to glucose ingestion depends upon both nervous and humoral mechanisms.
the insulin response to oral glucose ingestion is not only determined by the blood glucose rise but is also influenced by a nervous trigger and the load-dependent humoral potentiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

transplantation of a neonatal rat pancreas under the kidney capsule in an adult alloxan diabetic rat restores the ability of the transplanted pancreas to release insulin in response to glucose ingestion, but not in response to nervous stimulation.

transplantation of neonatal pancreatic islets under the kidney capsule in the rat results in normal glucose tolerance and normal insulin response to oral glucose ingestion, but that the normal anticipatory insulin response to glucose ingestion is lost, and that the load dependent insulin response to glucose is reduced.
the transplantation of a neonatal pancreas to the diabetic rat results in a normal insulin secretion in response to glucose ingestion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it’s not just about what you eat, but also how you eat it.
the insulin response to oral glucose is load dependent and that a nervous trigger of the early phase insulin secretion is present in normal animals but lacking in transplanted rats.
the pancreas is not just a glucose sensing organ.
